newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian minister defends military reform.
newsitem.headline: Russian minister defends military reform.

text.p: Russian Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev, countering an attack from a respected general on his plans for military reform, said on Friday there was no other way to save Russia's struggling armed forces from utter collapse.

Sergeyev compared an outspoken public attack on the Kremlin's military policy by General Lev Rokhlin, a senior pro-government legislator, to Bolshevik agitation in the military which helped the communists seize power in Russia in 1917.

"By 2001 the army will become completely ineffective, uncontrollable and disarmed if we go on without radical change," the former strategic command chief said in an interview in the Defence Ministry daily newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda (Red Star).

Since the fall of Soviet communism in 1991 the army has been dogged by chronic cash shortages. Officers often go months without pay and underfed conscripts have been reduced to begging in the streets. Suicide, theft, murder and bullying of young recruits by senior officers have become commonplace.

President Boris Yeltsin, outraged by the dramatic decline of the huge but largely ineffective military machine, put Sergeyev in charge of the ministry last month, ordering him to start long-delayed military reforms.

Yeltsin has said he wants the armed forces to be cut to 1.2 million troops from about 1.8 million as part of a long-term strategy to transform the ramshackle, conscript-based forces into a leaner, professional fighting machine.

In an open address to Yeltsin published on Tuesday, Rokhlin, a member of the pro-government Our Home is Russia party and chairman of the parliamentary defence committee, said that Yeltsin's military reform would finally ruin the armed forces.
Rokhlin, a popular figure in the military, also appealed to army officers to stand up for their rights and to resist government plans to scale down the military.
Sergeyev described Rokhlin's appeal as "totally unacceptable and provocative".
"Let us try to learn from our own history," said Sergeyev, who has a reputation as an intellectual among the top brass.

"Let us remember the awful result of Bolshevik agitation in the Russian army in 1917. Everyone knows how it all ended," he said. During World War One, much of Russia's demoralised military backed the successful Bolshevik coup d'etat.

Sergeyev said that the reform was meant to make the armed forces an effective instrument to face Russia's new security challenges and also to make military service attractive for both officers and other ranks.
He admitted that many officers would lose jobs as a result but said this was inevitable and promised to help them make the transition to civilian careers.
Shrugging off accusations that reforms were being prepared by civilians behind the backs of the military, Sergeyev said his plan had been coordinated with all top officers.
"My report to the president has just a few pages but it incorporates the efforts of many people," he said.
"Before presenting it to the president it has received the support of all deputy ministers, commanders of all branches of the forces and approved by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin."
Sergeyev urged soldiers to contribute to the reforms and even offered an address -- K-160, 103160 Moscow -- for them to write in with their suggestions.
